forces.title: Rising AI token usage offsets falling model prices for telcos
forces.description: Despite a tenfold annual decline in AI model prices, telcos face ballooning total token bills as usage rises. This occurs because employees discover new uses, power users consume tokens at scale (especially in network operations and customer care), tasks become more complex, and teams shift to newer, token-intensive models. Managing AI spending like cloud infrastructure, rather than by business outcome, risks unchecked expenditure and substantial unrealized savings for telecom operators.
forces.source_title: AI in Telecom: The Opex Reckoning

forces.title: Ineffective AI deployment by bolting onto legacy processes
forces.description: Many telcos deploy AI without fundamentally redesigning existing workflows, resulting in a dual operating model where AI performs isolated tasks while traditional teams continue legacy processes. This approach automates fragments of complexity rather than transforming operations end-to-end, leading to continued growth in SaaS licenses and AI becoming merely another line item. This prevents significant operational evolution and traps organizations in optimizing outdated processes with new technology, hindering competitive positioning for telecom operators.
forces.source_title: AI in Telecom: The Opex Reckoning

forces.title: Low ambition in AI adoption misses P&L upside
forces.description: Telcos often focus on low-risk AI demonstrations, such as internal chatbots or auto-generated call summaries, which yield only marginal efficiency improvements and fail to reshape a telco’s economics. This conservative approach misses the P&L upside from using AI to solve previously too-slow, too-manual, or too-expensive customer problems, such as autonomous network incident resolution or proactive churn prevention. Setting ambition too low prevents transformative change and leaves significant economic value unrealized.
forces.source_title: AI in Telecom: The Opex Reckoning

forces.title: AI to enable autonomous network operations for telcos
forces.description: AI can transform telecom network operations by redesigning detect-to-resolve workflows, enabling AI to detect anomalies, diagnose causes, execute corrective actions, validate outcomes, and escalate only when necessary. This shift from isolated activities to complete, closed-loop processes significantly reduces manual intervention and accelerates incident resolution. Such capabilities extend AI's reach into currently intractable optimization problems, positioning carriers for autonomous network operations and driving substantial efficiency gains and competitive advantage.
forces.source_title: AI in Telecom: The Opex Reckoning

forces.title: AI enables new customer experiences and self-service models
forces.description: AI allows telecom operators to address customer problems that were previously too slow, manual, or expensive to solve, fundamentally reshaping customer engagement. Examples include proactive churn prevention, personalized B2B proposal generation, and fully self-service retail experiences in economically unviable locations. This capability opens new markets and improves customer satisfaction by making previously unfeasible services economically viable, as demonstrated by Telia's AI-enabled kiosks in rural communities, driving growth and competitive differentiation.
forces.source_title: AI in Telecom: The Opex Reckoning

forces.title: Continuous investment required for innovation and efficiency in Irish telecom
forces.description: The Irish Computers & Telecoms sector is characterized by a relentless pace of innovation and efficiency-driven technological change, which structurally demands ongoing investment from market participants. Companies must continuously invest in innovation, cyber resilience, and workforce capabilities to remain competitive. This permanent need for capital expenditure and strategic planning is a fundamental aspect of operating in this fast-moving market, driving continuous evolution in business models and operational practices for telecom service providers.

forces.title: Global trade and investment shifts pose risks to Irish telecom
forces.description: Irish telecom companies face medium-impact risks from evolving global trade dynamics, including potential US tariff developments, reshoring initiatives, and shifts in multinational investment decisions. Any significant change in global strategies could adversely affect supply chains, hiring activity, and future capital expenditure within Ireland's technology and telecom sectors. This necessitates close monitoring of international policy and corporate movements to mitigate potential disruptions and maintain the country's position as a technology hub.

forces.title: Surging data center demand drives need for fiber connectivity
forces.description: The rapid growth of AI workloads is fueling a surge in data center capital expenditures, creating a strong and sustained demand for high-speed fiber connectivity. AI data centers are highly networked assets, requiring dense fiber networks and proximity to major users. This creates a significant tailwind for fixed-line and fiber telecom operators (IN090102) as they are essential providers of the underlying network infrastructure, benefiting from increased demand for high-bandwidth services and new installations to support these power-intensive facilities.
forces.source_title: Colocation data centers: The infrastructure race behind AI

forces.title: Grid connection delays impact data center and supporting infrastructure
forces.description: Lead times for grid connection to data centers are a significant bottleneck, averaging over four years and potentially extending up to a decade in some markets. This impacts the ability to bring new data center capacity online, and consequently, the deployment of necessary fiber and network infrastructure by telecom operators (IN090102). These delays increase construction costs and extend build times, limiting how quickly high-demand connectivity services can be expanded even in otherwise advantaged markets like London and Paris.
forces.source_title: Colocation data centers: The infrastructure race behind AI

forces.title: Post-quantum cryptography urgency due to 'harvest now, decrypt later' threat
forces.description: Telecom carriers face an immediate and critical risk from 'harvest now, decrypt later' threats, where nation-state actors are harvesting encrypted data today, anticipating future decryption with quantum computers. This makes post-quantum cryptography (PQC) a top priority, as the risks associated with harvested data could last for decades. Carriers must identify, assess, and migrate cryptographic dependencies across their entire estate by 2030 to protect sensitive sovereign data, financial transactions, and critical infrastructure signaling.
forces.source_title: How Telecom Carriers Are Preparing for Quantum

forces.title: Complex PQC migration for telcos across 5G, SIMs, and infrastructure
forces.description: Migrating to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) presents unique and high complexity for telecom carriers. It requires coordinated equipment vendor upgrades across the entire 5G core and RAN, updating cryptographic keys for hundreds of millions of SIMs without service disruption, and hardware acceleration for transport layer security at carrier-grade throughput. The hardening regulatory clock, with the European Commission pushing for critical infrastructure PQC readiness by 2030, adds significant pressure, making discovery and migration an urgent, multi-year undertaking.
forces.source_title: How Telecom Carriers Are Preparing for Quantum

forces.title: Quantum computing to optimize complex telecom network challenges
forces.description: Quantum computing holds significant potential to optimize complex telecom network challenges that exceed classical algorithms. This includes network planning, fiber route optimization (already demonstrated by Vodafone), RAN optimization (beamforming, interference management, Cloud RAN resource provisioning), and energy management across thousands of cell sites. While the technology is maturing towards a critical threshold of 100 stable logical qubits around 2028–2029, building internal capabilities now allows carriers to gain a competitive advantage from future efficiencies of 30-40% in cost structures.
forces.source_title: How Telecom Carriers Are Preparing for Quantum

forces.title: Telcos' fiber ownership provides advantage in quantum communications
forces.description: Telecom carriers possess a structural advantage in quantum communications, particularly Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), due to their extensive fiber infrastructure ownership. This allows them to offer targeted, high-security solutions for high-value segments like government, finance, healthcare, and critical infrastructure where provable security commands a premium. Commercial deployments by BT/Toshiba, SK Telecom, Orange, and Deutsche Telekom demonstrate QKD's viability at metro scale, positioning carriers with fiber assets as key players in emerging sovereign security propositions.
forces.source_title: How Telecom Carriers Are Preparing for Quantum

forces.title: Higher energy costs pressure telecom margins due to geopolitical crises
forces.description: Telecoms services, while not directly exposed to the Middle East crisis, face significant indirect pressure from increased European gas prices, which translate into higher electricity costs. For data centers and telecom networks, energy costs are a core input. Rising prices erode margins and can delay investment decisions, dampening expansion appetite across the sector. This heightened geopolitical risk and energy price volatility necessitates careful cost management and resilience planning to protect profitability and growth strategies for telecom operators.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

forces.title: Geopolitical instability elevates cybersecurity risks for critical infrastructure
forces.description: Geopolitical instability contributes to heightened cybersecurity risks, prompting 38% of Irish organizations to reassess critical infrastructure locations and 41% to increase cyber insurance coverage. For telecom carriers, managing national communications infrastructure and sensitive data, this translates to an elevated threat environment. State-sponsored cyberattacks and increased threat personas demand robust resilience planning, heightened investment in cybersecurity measures, and potential re-evaluation of infrastructure locations to protect against disruptions and maintain service integrity.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

viewpoints.title: Telcos face significant operating cost shift and risk from AI adoption
viewpoints.description: Bain forecasts a major shift in telco operating costs over the next 3-5 years as AI agents become embedded across various functions. An 'agentic operating model' could see AI agent and token costs comprise 20-30% of total opex. However, telcos risk increasing total operating expenses without proportional gains in productivity, customer experience, or growth if they merely layer AI onto legacy systems without fundamental workflow redesign and proactive cost management, necessitating immediate strategic action.
viewpoints.source_title: AI in Telecom: The Opex Reckoning

viewpoints.title: Ireland's Computers & Telecoms sector maintains low risk and stable conditions
viewpoints.description: Allianz Ireland assesses the Computers & Telecoms sector in Ireland as low risk in H1 2026, citing stable trading conditions and strong underlying performance. The sector benefits from robust multinational investment and consistent demand for talent, with insolvencies remaining low. However, continuous investment in innovation, cyber resilience, and workforce capability is essential to remain competitive amidst rapid technological change and potential global strategic shifts affecting supply chains.

viewpoints.title: Telecoms poised for fast AI adoption and significant value capture
viewpoints.description: McKinsey identifies the telecommunications sector as digitally mature, enabling rapid AI adoption due to rich data, high margins, and standardized processes. This foundation allows telcos to deploy vertical AI agents efficiently. A European media and telecommunications company, for example, projected £1.4 billion in five-year net present value from over 250 GenAI use cases, underscoring the substantial financial and operational value AI can unlock across the sector through efficiency and new service development.

viewpoints.title: Quantum technology poses immediate, outsized challenge for telcos
viewpoints.description: Bain highlights quantum technology as an immediate and significant challenge for telecom carriers, with implications for network security, infrastructure strategy, and regulation. Carriers must differentiate between post-quantum cryptography (PQC), quantum computing, and quantum communications, as each demands distinct timelines and organizational responses. Conflating these risks either premature overinvestment or dangerous complacency, especially given the active threat posed by 'harvest now, decrypt later' scenarios for PQC.
viewpoints.source_title: How Telecom Carriers Are Preparing for Quantum

viewpoints.title: Ireland's AI adoption in workplaces surpasses EU average but governance lags
viewpoints.description: According to the AI Economy in Ireland 2026 report (Trinity College, Dublin), Ireland's AI adoption rates exceed the EU average, with 43% of private-sector organizations actively using AI tools. Adoption is comparable across all enterprise sizes. This indicates a strong move from AI intention to execution. However, governance and oversight remain challenges, as only 43.6% of respondents have formal AI policies in place, suggesting a need for more robust frameworks to manage widespread deployment.
viewpoints.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

demand_drivers.description: AI automates, augments, and robotizes existing work, and enables better products, higher output, faster innovation, personalization, and new services within telecom operations.

pnl_drivers.description: AI automates tasks and improves existing work, leading to 6-9% value improvement through reduced effort and cost in telecom operations.

pnl_drivers.driver: Revenue growth from new products and services
pnl_drivers.description: AI enables better products, faster innovation, personalization, and new business models for telecom services, leading to 3-6% value improvement.

new_opportunities.description: A European media and telecommunications company identified over 250 generative AI use cases with a potential £1.4 billion in five-year net present value. This indicates substantial opportunities for telcos to leverage AI across their operations, from customer service and network management to product development, driving significant financial upside through efficiency gains and new service offerings.
new_opportunities.opportunity: Gen AI use cases for significant net present value

market_sizing.methodology: Estimated 5-year Net Present Value (NPV) from over 250 identified GenAI use cases within a single European media and telecommunications company, reflecting potential industry gains.

pnl_drivers.driver: Shift in operating expense structure due to AI
pnl_drivers.description: Over the next 3-5 years, telcos' operating cost structures will significantly shift. An 'agentic operating model' is emerging where AI agent and token costs are expected to constitute 20-30% of total operating expenditures, with traditional opex making up the remaining 70-80%. This introduces a new cost component and necessitates careful management to avoid cost-creep and ensure proportional productivity gains for telecom operators.

market_sizing.methodology: Analysis of projected shifts in operating cost structure for telecom operators due to AI integration over a three-to-five-year horizon.
market_sizing.source_title: AI in Telecom: The Opex Reckoning

new_opportunities.description: The broader 'Telecoms/Tech Services' sector in Ireland saw increased venture capital investment in Q1 2026, with 15 deals (up from 13 in Q1'25) and significant investor interest, particularly in AI. This indicates growing M&A activity and capital inflow, especially in subsectors like cybersecurity, creating opportunities for telecom service providers to acquire capabilities, innovate, or benefit from strategic investment in associated technologies and solutions.
new_opportunities.opportunity: Increased VC investment and M&A in Telecoms/Tech Services

market_sizing.methodology: Q1 2026 M&A deal count for the broader 'Telecoms/Tech Services' sector in Ireland, showing 15 deals, up from 13 in Q1 2025, with strong investor interest in AI.
